newsitem.title: UK: Britain orders new research into Gulf War syndrome.
newsitem.headline: Britain orders new research into Gulf War syndrome.

text.p: Britain's Labour government on Monday announced a new research programme into the mysterious ailments suffered by many veterans of the Gulf War and promised to speed up assessments of their condition.

The announcement was greeted by ex-soldiers as a victory in their campaign for official recognition of "Gulf War Syndrome", which they link to preparations for the 1991 war to drive Iraqi forces out of Kuwait.

The government said it planned a 2.5 million pound ($4.2 million) research programme into the possible health effects of the combination of vaccines and tablets given to Gulf War troops to protect them against chemical and biological warfare, and against desert insects.

Veterans say the syndrome results from a cocktail of chemicals administered to troops, and that it has caused problems such as asthma, chronic fatigue, depression and skin ailments. Some maintain it has resulted in serious birth defects in their children.
The government programme will be supervised by an independent panel of experts including a representative of the Gulf veterans, Armed Forces Minister John Reid told parliament.

"We have a duty to discharge our responsibilities in respect of those who have served their country. I aim to see we do just that," said Reid, who earlier had a lunch meeting with veterans' representatives.
About 51,000 Britons served in the Gulf War and up to 4,000 veterans or members of their families are ill.

Veterans have claimed for years that evidence gathered in the United States, whose troops were also involved in the Gulf War, supports the theory that the "cocktail" of immunisations and pills may be responsible for the syndrome.
"This announcement is long overdue," said Tony Flint, coordinator of the National Gulf Veterans and Families Association.
"We have been banging our head against a brick wall for the last few years. Now that brick wall has come down."

Labour, which ended 18 years of Conservative rule by winning an election on May 1, had accused the previous government's policy of dragging its feet on research into Gulf War syndrome and compensation for veterans.
The Conservative government had insisted there was no single cause to explain the illnesses and attributed them to the stress of the war.
Reid said his government would continue to pay war pensions to those disabled because of the Gulf War, and that if further research showed liability, it would pay compensation.
He also promised to speed up the Defence Ministry's Medical Assessment Programme which assesses Gulf War veterans' ailments.
"The Ministry of Defence will make available to the public any information it possesses which is of potential relevance to this issue," he added.
